cover.alt: The household celebrates Christmas at Hamrar; the children receive shoes and candles, and Þórunn tells Ásta about the jólasveinar.
cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour, established character bible, Christmas 1874 in the baðstofa at Hamrar, Jökuldalur. Low turf-house interior with beds along the walls, lit fish-oil lamp and small tallow candles. Six-year-old Ásta wears plain new Icelandic sheepskin shoes and listens wide-eyed to Þórunn whispering beside the spinning wheel. A thin round cut-patterned laufabrauð wafer lies on a wooden board. Hallur, fully clothed in worn woollen travelling clothes, has just entered with snow on his coat. Guðrún stands by the children; Helga tends the candles and Siggi helps. Warm modest light, no modern furniture, no red Santa suit, no gifts other than shoes and candles, no lettering.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: „Í dag koma jólin!“ segir Ásta. Hún fær nýja skó og kerti.
Þórunn segir: „Á jólunum koma jólasveinarnir af fjöllunum.“
Séra Þorvaldur segir „jól“ í kirkjunni, og hann segir frá Kristi.
Afi segir „jól“, og hann skoðar Eddu. „Orðið er gamalt,“ segir hann, „eins og Ísland.“
words_with_history.note_en: Jól is older than Christianity in Iceland: it named a midwinter feast in heathen times, and the Church kept the word for Christmas. So the priest and afi can say the same word and think of different things.

pronunciation_note.rule: At the start of hvað and hver, hv- is usually pronounced [kv]. Listen for the same opening in hverjum.

grammar.title: mér · þér · honum · henni
grammar.rule: Guðrún gefur börnunum kerti. Siggi gefur henni kertið. Óðinn gefur úlfunum matinn.

grammar.note_en:
The subject is who or what does something. An object is a person or thing affected by the verb. In “Guðrún gives the children candles”, candles is the direct object: the thing given. The children is the indirect object: the recipients. Icelandic marks these jobs with case, the form of a noun, name or pronoun. The accusative is the direct-object case after gefa, “give”; the dative marks its recipient. These are sentence jobs, not merely places in a word order.

Guðrún gefur börnunum kerti (s012) means “Guðrún gives the children candles”. Guðrún is the subject, kerti the accusative direct object, and börnunum the dative recipient. Hún gefur Sigga skó, og hún gefur Ástu skó (s006) means “She gives Siggi shoes, and she gives Ásta shoes”. The recipient can stand before the thing given. Siggi tekur kertið og gefur henni það (s035) means “Siggi takes the candle and gives it to her”. Ég gef þér kertið mitt (s036) means “I give you my candle”. Óðinn gefur úlfunum matinn (s081) means “Óðinn gives the wolves his food”. Hún gefur fólkinu kjöt í askana (s091) means “She gives the people meat into the bowls”. Manga gefur Ástu það (s100) means “Manga gives it to Ásta”; hún gefur Möngu kjötið aftur (s101), “she gives Manga the meat back”. Matinn and kjötið are accusative definite objects: “the food”, “the meat”. The giving diagram beside s081 shows these three roles.

The first table pairs known nominative pronouns, used for subjects, with their dative forms. Ég → mér is “I → me”; þú → þér, “you → (to) you”; hann → honum, “he → him”; hún → henni, “she → her”; við → okkur, “we → us”; þið → ykkur, “you all → you all”; þeir → þeim, “they → them”. These pronouns do not share one ending: learn the encountered forms together with their sentence jobs. The nominative labels are already known from earlier chapters; the citations identify this chapter’s dative occurrences, including ykkur even though nobody says nominative þið in this chapter. Hún hjálpar honum (compare s055) means “she helps him”; fylgir þú mér? (s030), “are you following me?”; Nú segir þú okkur það, Hallur (s066), “Now you tell us that, Hallur”; Ég segi ykkur það (s067), “I tell you all that”; Hvað gefur hann þeim að borða? (s057), “What does he give them to eat?” In the last question, them means the men with Óðinn. Segja can take a dative addressee: the thing said is það, “that”, and the listeners are okkur or ykkur.

A verb can require a dative object even when English does not use “to”. Learn hjálpa + dative, “help”; fylgja + dative, “follow, go with”; and svara + dative, “answer”. Siggi hjálpar henni (s015) means “Siggi helps her”, where her is Helga. Ásta fylgir henni (s029) means “Ásta follows her”, again Helga. Helga vill hjálpa honum (s055) means “Helga wants to help him”, Siggi. Enginn svarar henni (s097) means “Nobody answers her”, Ásta. Siggi hjálpar honum; Svo fylgir hann Halli út (s128) means “Siggi helps him; then he goes out with Hallur”. Snati fylgir honum að túninu (s130) means “Snati follows him to the homefield”. Helping and following do not have an unspoken second object: these verbs simply select the dative.

By contrast, skoða, “look at”, and sjá, “see”, select the accusative. Ásta skoðar hann (s010) means “Ásta looks at him”, Hallur; Allir skoða hann (s044), “Everyone looks at him”, Siggi; Ásta skoðar Möngu (s101), “Ásta looks at Manga”; Hallur skoðar Sigga (s129), “Hallur looks at Siggi”. Við sjáum það ekki (s109) means “We do not see it”, the hidden people. English “look at” has a preposition, but Icelandic skoða does not. The verb’s own pattern decides the case.

The name forms must also be learned: Siggi → Sigga, Ásta → Ástu, Manga → Möngu, Hallur → Halli in the dative. Siggi loses final -i and takes -a; Ásta replaces final -a with -u; Manga does the same, with a → ö in the stem: Möngu. Hallur loses nominative -ur and takes dative -i: Halli. The accusative of Hallur is Hall, encountered after við in s051 and skoðar in s082; it differs from Halli. Sigga, Ástu and Möngu happen to be both accusative and dative, so the verb or preposition tells you their case. Börnum is the dative plural of barn; with the article it is börnunum, “the children”. Úlfar has dative plural úlfum; with the article it becomes úlfunum, “the wolves”: the final -m of -um drops before -num. Fólk has dative fólki; the definite form is fólkinu, “the people”. The neuter dative article is -nu: fólki + -nu → fólkinu. These noun endings are the same ones met for place phrases; now they mark recipients too.

Þér has two readings. Here it is the dative of singular þú, “(to) you”: Siggi gives a candle to Ásta in s036; Hallur speaks of the book hjá þér, “with you”, to Siggi in s129; afi will tell Siggi the story in s135. In Kafli 8, nominative þér is the formal “you” used to the priest and paired with a second-person plural verb. Context decides: giving something þér marks a recipient; formal þér is a subject. This chapter’s þér is not formal address.

Við also has two jobs. As a subject it means “we”: Nú sofum við (s045), “Now we sleep”; Af hverju erum við ekki í Valhöll? (s096), “Why are we not in Valhöll?”; við sjáum það ekki (s109), “we do not see it”. As a preposition here it takes an accusative: við rokkinn (s019, s104), “by the spinning wheel”; við hurðina (s025, s128), “by the door”. Segir hann við Hall (s051) means “he says to Hallur”: segja við + accusative is a different construction from segja + dative. Both can name the addressee. A preposition can also mean “against” in other contexts; none of these occurrences describes pushing against anything.

Mér er kalt (s003), “I am cold”, and Mig langar í göltinn (s095), “I want / long for the boar”, are supported whole expressions. In the first, the person is mér; in the second, mig. Do not replace one with the other or try to build a general subject-case system yet; that comes at G19. They are explained here but are not tabulated or blanked in the exercises. Sjáðu, “look”, Getur þú það?, “can you do it?”, eins og, “like”, and skelfur, “shakes”, likewise remain supported items rather than drill targets. Þá segi ég þér það (s135) means “Then I will tell you that”: Icelandic uses the present segi for this future occasion. No past tense or new future ending is introduced.
